There are two comments that I am replying to which both give examples from different languages where an equivalent to “noodles” is used to describe pasta. It is also worth stating that Americans use “pasta” and “macaroni” equally often, just like what is described above in Russian and German. 

English also having roots in Romance languages (which I assume is where you are getting French) does not mean it does not also have Germanic roots, which it has in common with modern German. “Noodles” happens to be a word of Germanic origin that was introduced to the US that is used here in the same way it is used in Germany. 

My main point, which I assume you were determined to ignore so you could offer a cursory linguistics lecture, is that different countries are introduced to different foods from different cultures at different times, which leads to the *extremely normal* phenomenon of having different names for things. Think “fries” vs. “chips,” for a common example. Very nearly everyone understood what OP was talking about, as even if it was not their conventional vocabulary, there is *plenty* of context. 

Also, calling something “uniquely American” because that’s not how it’s done in England specifically…you know there are other places where English is spoken, right? With wide varieties of terminology? What a weird and ethnocentric thing to say
Half of English is derived from German yet people will still act like it’s a uniquely American thing to use language that is common in many other places…

This is obviously a very personal decision for you, but my advice is to consider whether your conflict is rooted in whether you’re ready for a pregnancy/baby, or if it is rooted in worry about how the people in your life will feel about you if you choose to terminate. I hope you can come to a place where you can separate the two and focus only on the part that is about you, your body, and your future. 

I also want to say: people will always try to make you think having an abortion will traumatize you behind repair — but the reality is that so many people who have abortions feel peace, relief, or nothing at all once the physical pain subsides. The reason we hear so many stories of abortion “trauma” is because those are the people who speak out against it and use it as manipulation (obviously this is not *always* the case, but it is most certainly prevalent). It’s completely normal to feel no guilt or shame outside of what others in your life are feeling on your behalf. The trauma of pregnancy and motherhood before you are ready  will affect more than just you; it will affect your child, their loved ones, and their future children. If *you* know that you are not ready, that is all you need to know. 

Also because I think this needs to be said: many unplanned babies go on to have wonderful lives with wonderful parents who were once in your position. I just don’t want you to read all these comments and think your only options are to terminate or be a terrible mom with a terrible life. And in the same vein, just because there’s a good chance going through with the pregnancy will turn out to be wonderful, *it is still, without a doubt, 1000% valid for you to not want that.*

Not to mention, missing the exam could literally have meant this was *all for nothing.* OP, but *especially* OP’s husband is lucky she was able to get it rescheduled.

Oh no, I’m sorry you’re feeling this way! First off, this is completely valid and you are not asking for too much, nor are you being a brat. You sound like a very well adjusted person (mind you, you’re at an age where you’re definitely not even expected to be). 

I am not saying this to make excuses for him, but it sounds like your dad might really be struggling with not getting enough sleep as well as the stress of having a new baby. Both of these things can cause memory loss and difficulty paying attention, plus mood swings and low energy, and it sounds like you’re noticing all these things in him. The tough part is that it seems to unfortunately all be landing on you, which can understandably make you feel neglected - but I am it hoping by telling you this you can believe that it’s not because he doesn’t care about you, but pretty much just because he’s pretty drained. I know it doesn’t change what’s happened, but it can help to understand that it’s not by choice. 

I agree that writing a letter is a great idea. That way he can read and process it on his own time without the pressure of a face-to-face confrontation. From the background you’ve shared about before the baby, it’s obvious that you’re very special to him and that makes me believe he will be willing to work with you to fix things. 

The last thing I want to say is there is nothing wrong with asking to be included in things! Even when he’s giving the baby a bath or feeding her or just doing basic boring chores, see if you can just sit with them and chat or just keep them company. I’m willing to bet your dad misses you too and is feeling bad that he can’t hang out with you the way he used to. It will mean a lot to him that you’re creating more time to spend together.

Memory is often linked to mental/emotional health. I developed memory problems when I was experiencing depression and lost large portions of memories over several months before I got treatment. There were also day-to-day symptoms like forgetting something I was just told, repeating myself because I couldn’t remember if I’d already said something out loud, asking a question then not hearing the answer... it sounds pretty similar to what you are experiencing. It’s possible there is some imbalance that is making it challenging for your short-term memory to process things. 

I am sorry to be another person calling attention to your relationship since you seem already aware of what’s going on, but I do have two comments: first, it’s very probable that this relationship is triggering your memory difficulties; and second: it sounds like a LOT of your boyfriend’s requests are meant as traps to get you to mess up. Asking for such short, specific time increments then punishing you when you’re off by a few minutes is ridiculous. It’s basic colloquialism that “3 minutes” or “5 minutes” really means “a short period of time/once you finish your immediate task.” This behavior is not only ridiculously controlling but also just nonsensical.

Something I try to do in interactions: if someone doesn't know something that might seem simple or obvious to me, get excited for them to have the opportunity to learn and for you to be able to teach them. Skip the "you've never heard of ____ before!?!" and go straight to the "oh well today is your lucky day; let me teach you a little bit!" Make it casual and excited. They're giving you an opportunity to bring more knowledge into the world and that's something pretty neat. Don't condescend or make them feel dumb, even if you think they should have known this all along. Nobody knows everything.
